items.abstract: Leveraging the relaxation of fertility policies as a natural experiment, we examine the motherhood-related constraints faced by female directors and their effects on corporate risk-taking. Using a difference-in-differences design with director-level data, we find that firms with a higher proportion of childbearing-age female directors exhibit significant increases in corporate risk-taking following the policy reform. Consistent with an anticipatory discrimination channel, the increase is more pronounced when female directors hold less power, suggesting that fertility-related expectations may weaken their effective influence in board decision-making. Director-level analyses also document lower in-person board meeting attendance among potentially exposed female directors, providing behavioral evidence consistent with caregiving-related constraints on direct board participation. Cross-sectional analyses indicate that the effect is stronger in firms with weaker ESG performance and in regions where Confucian and clan-based cultural norms are less influential. Higher-exposure firms also increase both capital expenditure intensity and R&D intensity, are more likely to initiate M&A activity, and reduce cash holdings. We further find suggestive evidence of lower subsequent firm value, particularly when post-policy increases in risk-taking are greater. Overall, our findings highlight how fertility policy reform can interact with gendered expectations surrounding motherhood and constrain female directors’ professional participation and influence, with consequences for corporate risk-taking and shareholder value. This study contributes to business ethics by showing how fertility policies can perpetuate inequities in corporate governance and shape organizational outcomes.
items.title: The Penalty of Anticipated Motherhood in the Boardroom: Fertility Policy and Corporate Risk-Taking

items.abstract: Abstract Although a given mathematical theorem can typically be proved in many ways, only some of those proofs are regarded by mathematicians as explaining why that theorem holds. Furthermore, mathematicians routinely use non-deductive arguments to confirm conjectures before they have found proofs (or disproofs) of them. These two features of mathematical practice suggest that some confirmation in mathematics proceeds by “inference to the best explanation” (IBE). Furthermore, a mathematical theorem may exhibit a striking symmetry, and a proof of such a theorem would have to exploit a similar symmetry in order to explain why that theorem holds. This aspect of mathematical explanation reveals an important, heretofore unrecognized form of IBE in mathematics. In such a case, a conjecture is confirmed by some mathematical discovery partly because the conjecture “perfects the symmetry” in that discovery. This paper examines one historical example of such an IBE: Brahmagupta and Snell (independently) regarded Heron’s formula for the area of triangles as confirming a conjecture not merely because that conjecture generalizes Heron’s formula, but also because that conjecture perfects the formula’s symmetry.
items.title: Perfecting the symmetry: a variety of inference to the best explanation in mathematics

items.abstract: Abstract The concept of the self is the concept of what makes a person the person that they are. But how can a general, theoretical account be given of something that is, by definition, specific to each individual? Discussions of selfhood in the analytic tradition have focused on three different issues: (1) self-reference in language and thought, (2) the epistemology of self-knowledge, (3) the metaphysics/ontology of selves. These are all connected to each other and all important. But even if we had satisfactory answers to all of them, we would have at best an account of the formal conditions of selfhood, rather than of selfhood itself. Focusing primarily on ancient Greece, this paper explores an alternative approach to thinking about selfhood. Individuality, selfhood, can only be expressed within certain limits and certain structures. When we look at historical texts, if we seek to find an author’s conception of the self, we need to tease out how they frame those factors that constrain and channel the development, articulation, and expression of selfhood - as opposed, for example, to looking at whatever metaphysical account they might give of the mind or of personhood (or of the uniquely Greek concept of the psuchē ).
items.title: What would count as a theory of the self?

items.abstract: Abstract Deontological arguments, in the broad sense, are those that refer to properties of choice options other than their consequences, such as whether the option is an act or omission. These arguments are often used to justify public policies, such as those concerning vaccination. In principle, some of these arguments could lead to outcomes worse than those of utilitarian choices, i.e., choices designed to yield the best expected consequences. Arguments for deontological choices ought to explain why it is better to make outcomes worse. We suggest that political arguments attempting to do this are usually fallacious. We list several categories of such informal fallacies, and we report two demonstrations in which we ask whether people without special training can distinguish types of such reasoning. People seem generally weak at this task, although those who are more inclined to accept the standards of actively open-minded thinking (AOT) do better, possibly because both AOT and fallacy classification require meta-cognitive competence. Performance may also be improved by more thorough instructions about the task. The idea of requesting justification for making things worse is a new method for empirical research on moral judgment and for instruction in argumentation. It is also a new kind of thought experiment for philosophical argument.
items.title: Recognizing fallacious reasoning in deontological arguments

items.abstract: We experience and appreciate together with others the beauty of a sunset or an artwork, the sadness of a musical piece. Admiring the same aesthetic properties of objects together with others is a ubiquitous human activity. At the same time, it is commonly held that aesthetic properties constitutively depend on a subjective response. This brings up a particular challenge: How can we jointly focus towards the same aesthetic property when it is itself dependent on our separate responses? In this paper, I provide an analysis of joint aesthetic attention and explain how we can engage in it. I propose a multiple coordinative profile: co-attenders coordinate their perceptual attention to the object, but also coordinate the specific way they attend to it, and their specific responsive profiles. I advance a novel capacities-based probabilistic account of how this multiple coordination is possible.
items.title: Joint aesthetic attention

items.abstract: Abstract This paper addresses a central phenomenological puzzle: how to reconcile the traditional view of compassion as an instance of suffering with contemporary neuroscientific findings characterizing it as being hedonically positive. Building on the attitudinalist framework, I argue that this conflict arises from a failure to see emotions as unfolding episodes. By thinking of emotions as felt readinesses to act, we can understand compassion’s valence not as a fixed hedonic tone, but as a dynamic trajectory within a structured affective space. The argument proceeds in three stages. First, I establish that positive and negative emotions are defined by their structural orientation, welcoming or rejecting value. Second, I apply this to compassion, arguing it is fundamentally a mode of taking displeasure in another’s suffering. Finally, I show that the “positivity” noted by scientists is the result of the benevolent action tendency being allowed to run its course, transforming initial distress into the expansive experience of relief and connection.
items.title: The Valence of Compassion

items.abstract: This paper examines the role of analogies in scientific discovery and proposes three criteria for evaluating their heuristic effectiveness. We contrast our approach with isolationist accounts of analogical arguments developed within argumentation theory. In particular, we examine Bartha’s Articulation Model, highlighting both its points of convergence with, and its divergences from, our own framework. Our approach focuses on the capacity of analogies to expand scientific knowledge in exploratory contexts, rather than assessing them as formal arguments. First, a successful analogy must possess an appropriate inferential structure, combining abductive hypothesis formation with deductive consequences and inductive testing. Second, an analogy must display asymmetry, insofar as the source domain is sufficiently well understood to justify inferences about the target. Finally, an analogy must be fruitful, generating explanatory or predictive consequences that motivate further empirical investigation. The usefulness of these criteria is illustrated through three historical cases. Darwin’s cluster of analogies, Paley’s design analogy and Kepler’s account of planetary motion. The proposed framework offers a historically informed account of the epistemic and heuristic value of analogies in science.
items.title: Criteria for the Evaluation of Analogies in Scientific Discovery

items.abstract: Being told that an algorithm decided is not the same as being able to change what it decided. This article argues that people subject to consequential automated decisions are owed an effective opportunity to change them, on grounds of justification, non-domination and procedural justice, and that this opportunity exists only when seven guarantees are present for the individual decision: notice, reasons, access to the data used, correction, appeal, human review and remedy authority. It measures this chain in 28 legal instruments and 117,460 privacy policies with PROVE, a transparent provision extractor that separates disclosure of automated decision-making (ADM) from denials and rights recitals (held-out micro-F1 against human coding 0.65; keyword matching 0.23). Of 4303 policies that mention ADM, 259 disclose using it. Among these, 51% give affirmative notice, 17% explain the decision logic, 23% offer a way to contest, 19% promise human involvement, and fewer than 1% give access to or correction of the data used or state that the reviewer may change the outcome. Explanation predicts appeal but not remedy, 81% of human-review promises say nothing about what the reviewer can do, and no policy completes the chain; in the express text of the law, only Colorado’s SB 26-189 and Quebec’s Law 25 do. Measured against the ethical standard, disclosures inform people without empowering them and promise human oversight without stating its authority, and those for credit, insurance and employment decisions are thinner than for lower-stakes ones. The chain turns contestability from a principle into a checkable standard.
items.title: Can people challenge an AI decision? Measuring the contestability chain in law and corporate disclosure

items.abstract: Research on model collapse has shown that generative AI models degrade when recursively trained on their own outputs, losing the tails of their distributions. That work addresses one pathway, machines degrading machines, and leaves the human side unexamined. This paper distinguishes two components of the human-side pathway: one internal to the interaction between a single user and a single system, and one environment-mediated, theorised here as stigmergic convergence : the process by which LLM outputs accumulate on the web and alter the knowledge base of non-users as well as users, through search results and ambient environments. Where the human-side and machine-side pathways proceed together, spiral detection failure would arise: the capacity to detect such change is itself degraded. Proposed countermeasures (real-data mixing, strategic human selection, provenance tracking) presuppose the integrity of that capacity and the non-contamination of reference data, neither of which can be structurally guaranteed. A four-layer closed-loop model is developed in which Layer 0 (RLHF preference convergence) already operates, while Layers 1, 2 and 2ʹ (cognitive drift, already-shaped human data entering training corpora, and detection tools and evaluators forming within that environment) are advanced as a hypothesised ordering, not an established result. Within this structure, the independence of any reference point for judging interventions must be confirmed. Set alongside the accountability vacuum described by Medsker and Virmani, this identifies a prior condition. Accountability operates on harms already detected and classified as harms, and it is that prior capacity the loop erodes. Beneath the accountability vacuum lies a detection vacuum.
items.title: The detection vacuum beneath the accountability vacuum: stigmergic convergence and spiral detection failure

items.abstract: The rapid adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) has exposed a critical gap in existing AI governance literature: the absence of an integrated model explaining how leaders and organizations build the decision-making capacities needed to enact ethical AI governance in practice. While frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and OECD AI Principles provide essential governance infrastructure, they do not address how leaders develop the judgment, adaptive capacity, and organizational learning required to act on that infrastructure. This paper addresses this gap by proposing a framework that integrates leadership capability, ethical reasoning, and organizational learning for AI governance across sectors. This research employs a conceptual synthesis approach to develop CALLOSSE (Complex Adaptive Leadership, Learning Organization, Sociotechnical Systems, and Ethics), drawing on Sociotechnical Systems Theory, Adaptive Leadership extended through DeRue’s complex adaptive process model, and Organizational Learning, with Ethics positioned as the foundational boundary condition governing all framework decisions. The study also adapts the Hourglass Model for AI governance [ 28 ] as the institutional architecture within which CALLOSSE operates, adding a Feedback and Learning layer, establishing a dual-pathway mechanism for routine operations and risk-triggered governance responses. CALLOSSE makes four specific contributions. First, it positions ethics as an active governance decision tool with a prioritized conflict-resolution logic rather than a compliance backdrop. Second, it applies Sociotechnical Systems Theory to diagnose how AI reshapes human-technology relationships, enabling leaders to understand consequences rather than only assign accountability. Third, it uses complex adaptive leadership to navigate the value conflicts and adaptive challenges that policy alone cannot resolve. Fourth, it embeds double-loop organizational learning as an endogenous governance mechanism, enabling organizations to revise the assumptions behind their AI policies over time. The four lenses interact through constraint, design translation, mediation, and institutionalization across four stages: Assessment, Design, Implementation, and Learning and Evaluation. CALLOSSE bridges governance architecture and leadership capability, supporting the development of calibrated trust—leaders’ capacity to assess when AI recommendations warrant acceptance and when human judgment should take precedence. This research contributes to ongoing dialogue on algorithmic accountability and offers a cross-sector, empirically testable approach for future research into values-based AI governance and leadership education.
items.title: Building AI-ethical competencies: an integrated framework for AI governance, organizational learning, and leadership education

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the proliferation of conversational agents have brought transformative changes in education but pose challenges in ensuring the academic integrity of assessments. This article proposes ‘affirmation vivas’ as a potent response to reasonable doubts about the authorship of assessed student work. It draws on a case-study of the first affirmation viva conducted at the University of Glasgow, conducted after ChatGPT “confessed” to generating part of a student dissertation. During the viva, while acknowledging experimenting with AI chatbots, the student successfully demonstrated understanding and ownership of their work. The article reviews practical and ethical issues involved in responding to suspected AI misuse and develops a principled framework for affirmation vivas. We conceptualise these vivas as a means of affirming student understanding rather than detecting AI misuse or presuming misconduct. We derive five principles for their fair and proportionate implementation, including a high threshold for convening them, a presumption of innocence throughout the process and for marking to take place only after the viva, avoiding biases that derive from assuming a student’s guilt.
items.title: Presumption of guilt? AI chatbots and the role of affirmation vivas in assessing academic integrity

items.abstract: Abstract The rise of agentic AI and so-called AI companions introduces a shift in the modes of interactions between humans and machines. The exact contours of this shift remain unclear, but early signs of social, affective, and even romantic engagements demonstrate areas of potential benefit and potent harms to individuals and to the broader social fabric. A full appreciation of these benefits and harms demands a multi-perspectival account not only of technological innovation and emerging modalities of human-machine interaction, but also of the historical, socio-cultural, psychological, and ethical aspects of companionship. This essay provides such as account through a pragmatist perspective that considers the material, institutional, and psycho-social conditions behind the rise of AI. From this perspective, the essay broadens the notion of “alignment” as one between means and ends rather than the commonly accepted formulation between design goals and outputs. We argue that AI companionship blurs the boundaries between tools and social actors—a dynamic that emerges from the interplay of technical architectures, intentional design practices, user psychology, and political-economic forces. Given that interplay, a set of interrelated questions arise, which we address in three clusters (supply, demand, mediation), highlighting the emerging social and ethical dilemmas, and suggesting pragmatic interventions to inform public discourse and policymaking. In so doing, we hope to curtail the tremendous fallouts that have become evident in other domains such as social media only in retrospect, and ​to contribute to the creation of an environment conducive to social cohesion and individual wellbeing.
items.title: AI companions, human concerns: a pragmatic perspective

items.abstract: Abstract The choice of legal basis of EU legal acts is a constitutional question in EU law, determining the relevant competence, institutional role, voting rule, related procedures, and issues of judicial review. This article advances a legal basis critique of a corpus of EU legal acts adopted in the past decade. As it demonstrates, the legal basis case-law set out by the Court of Justice of the European Union, and the limits of what particular legal bases permit, remain formally undisturbed. The practice of EU law, however, has demonstrably shifted, requiring sustained constitutional attention.
items.journal: Cambridge Yearbook of European Legal Studies
items.title: Legal Basis of EU Legal Acts: Choice, Doctrine, and Practice

items.abstract: Abstract The lack of affordable prescription medicines is a global problem. But even as various governments, nonprofit organizations and pharmaceutical companies attempt to address the issue, agreements lack transparency. The absence of key details — notably, pricing, in some instances — makes it difficult to determine whether the deals will sufficiently succeed in providing needed medicines.
items.title: What Details? A Lack of Transparency Impedes Access to Medicines

items.abstract: Abstract This paper offers the largest empirical study to date of the rights of persons with disabilities in the Commonwealth Caribbean. Drawing on interviews, surveys, focus groups and consultations conducted across twelve jurisdictions between 2017 and 2022, it examines the persistent gap between the region’s formal commitments under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the lived realities of persons with disabilities. Deploying Martha Nussbaum’s capability approach, alongside intersectional theory, the paper argues that pervasive failures across education, health care, employment, social protection, accessibility and civic participation deprive persons with disabilities of the substantive freedoms necessary for human flourishing, with compounded effects for those experiencing multiple forms of marginalisation. Situating these findings within the region’s heterogeneous legislative landscape, and assessing Barbados’s Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2025 as the region’s most far-reaching statutory response, the paper contends that transforming disability rights from aspiration into substantive capability requires structural change that addresses the intersection of ableism with racism, sexism, classism and geography.
items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
items.title: Disability rights in the Commonwealth Caribbean: a capability and intersectional critique

items.abstract: Abstract This article offers a comprehensive legal, linguistic, sociodemographic and psychological analysis of the phenomenon of mandatory fictitious paternity in civil status registration in Ukraine, as provided for in Part 1 of Article 135 of the Family Code of Ukraine. The study critically reassesses the Soviet legal legacy, which, through the prism of conceptual metaphors of ‘structural symmetry’, forces single mothers to enter non-existent data about the father, thereby creating administratively constructed paternal identities. Using a longitudinal analysis of this phenomenon from 2008 to 2025, the author demonstrates that the number of children at risk of administrative invisibility is approaching one million. Drawing on netnographic and autoethnographic methodologies, including cases of neurodivergent children, the article reveals the attendant psychosocial risks and critical barriers to the safety and mobility of Ukrainian refugee families in foreign jurisdictions during wartime. Based on these findings, the study conceptualises a model of moving beyond Soviet-era paternalistic registration practices in favour of documentary truth, advocating the introduction of the legal institution of the matronymic at the stage of primary registration.
items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
items.title: Legal fictions in birth registration: linguistic manifestations and social implications of paternity attribution in Ukraine and comparative perspectives

items.abstract: Abstract The article examines the challenges involved in restoring the rule of law in Poland. Under the rule of the Law and Justice (PiS) party from 2015 to 2023, Poland faced a profound constitutional crisis, marked by serious attacks on judicial independence. This crisis first affected the Constitutional Tribunal and later extended to the National Council of the Judiciary, whose unconstitutional politicization cast doubt on the legality of thousands of judicial appointments. Following the 2023 parliamentary elections, a new governing coalition assumed power, facing the complex challenge of rebuilding the Polish judiciary. The article outlines the guiding principles for the process of rule-of-law restoration and examines and assesses measures taken by the coalition government to resolve the crisis in the Polish judiciary. It is based on the assumption that the process of rule-of-law restoration must itself comply with the rule of law. Moreover, it argues that effectively resolving the crisis surrounding the Polish judiciary would require a meaningful political compromise involving the adoption of constitutional amendments to eliminate the roots of the crisis and increase the resilience of the constitutional system.
items.title: Lessons from the crisis: Rebuilding the Polish judiciary after the rule-of-law crisis

items.abstract: Abstract Epistemologists have recently argued that there is such a thing as ‘epistemic blame’: blame targeted at purely epistemic norm violations. Leading the charge has been Cameron Boult, who has argued across a papers and a monograph that we can make sense of this phenomenon by building an account of epistemic blame off of Scanlon’s account of moral blame. This paper argues a relationship-based account of epistemic blame is untenable, because it eliminates any distinction between blameworthy and excused agents. Attempts to overcome this problem cannot succeed because of the important but unrecognized ways his account deviates from Scanlon’s, and because of differences in how our moral and epistemic conduct are affected by our attitudes and expectations.
items.title: Epistemic blame isn’t relationship modification

items.abstract: Abstract In this paper, I analyse how and to what extent social structures constrain their occupants. To do so, I propose a 4-fold taxonomy of constraints: normative, conceptual, practical, and bodily constraints. They are distinguished by the nature of their binding force and by their existence conditions. For each type of constraint, I also analyse the strength of the limit that they can exert on our agency and examine whether they can be said to render certain options unavailable, rather than merely ill-advised or socially costly.
items.title: Social structural constraints and limits in the social world
